title: Prefabricated Home Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: Factory-built homes remain an affordability valve in a high-rate housing market, but shipments are flat-to-down while prices and consolidation keep revenue resilient.
overview: The industry produces factory-built housing and related prefabricated structures, led by HUD-code manufactured homes and modular or panelized residential buildings. The 2021 IBIS baseline described a mature, concentrated industry with 2021 revenue of $9.5 billion in 2021 dollars, 745 enterprises, 934 establishments, 48,447 employees and 9.1% profit margin. Current public data show the manufactured-housing core is larger in nominal terms but not strongly expanding in units: Census/FRED monthly shipments totaled 102,800 HUD-code homes in calendar 2025, down 0.6% from 103,400 in 2024, while the 2025 average manufactured-home sales price was $127,200, up 3.2% from $123,300 in 2024. Through May 2026, shipments were 41,400 homes, down 8.0% from 45,000 in January-May 2025, while the latest monthly average price was $134,800 in February 2026.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 manufactured-home shipment value proxy: $13.1 billion, calculated from 102,800 Census/FRED HUD-code shipments and $127,200 Census average sales price; 2024 IBIS-cited broader prefabricated home manufacturing market size was $13.3 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2025 shipment value proxy grew about 2.5% year over year as units fell 0.6% and average sales price rose 3.2%; January-May 2026 shipments fell 8.0% year over year to 41,400 homes.
key_stats.shipments: 102,800 HUD-code manufactured homes shipped in 2025; 41,400 shipped in January-May 2026.
key_stats.average_price: $127,200 average new manufactured-home sales price in 2025; $134,800 in February 2026.
key_stats.offsite_share: Modular and panelized construction accounted for 28,000 of 1,019,000 single-family completions in 2024, a 3% share, unchanged from 2023.
key_stats.mortgage_rate: Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 6.58% on August 21, 2025 and 6.48% on June 4, 2026.
key_stats.profitability: IBIS baseline profit margin was 9.1% in 2021; Champion Homes fiscal 2026 gross margin was 26.7% and Cavco fiscal 2026 factory-built housing gross margin was 22.1%, reflecting public-company gross margin rather than industry EBIT margin.

baseline_2022.market_size: IBIS baseline implied 2022 industry revenue of about $9.3 billion in 2021 dollars, applying its 2021-2027 projected CAGR of -1.87% to 2021 revenue of $9.5 billion; Census/FRED manufactured-home shipment value proxy was about $14.4 billion in 2022 from 113,100 shipments and $127,300 average price.
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS baseline outlook implied about -1.9% revenue growth in 2022; HUD-code shipment value rose sharply in 2022 because units reached 113,100 and average price rose to $127,300.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 9.1% in 2021 baseline, with IBIS forecasting 9.4% in 2026.
baseline_2022.employment: 48,447 employees in 2021 baseline, with IBIS forecasting 47,165 in 2026.
baseline_2022.establishments: 934 establishments in 2021 baseline; 2021-2027 establishment CAGR forecast was -0.38%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by designing and producing manufactured homes, modular homes, prefab wood buildings, ADUs, park models and nonresidential mobile buildings, then selling through independent dealers, company-owned retail centers, builders, developers, community operators, government buyers and wholesalers. Larger firms also capture downstream value from retail markup, setup, transport, construction services, consumer finance, floorplan lending and insurance.
cost_structure: Major costs are lumber and wood products, steel, gypsum, insulation, roofing, appliances, fixtures, chassis and transportation, plus direct plant labor, warranty reserves, dealer incentives, SG&A and compliance costs. Factory production lowers onsite labor exposure, but margins remain sensitive to lumber and steel swings, freight, financing costs, warranty events and plant utilization; BLS showed the softwood lumber cut-stock PPI at 101.276 in June 2026 versus 100.000 in May 2025.
major_players: Clayton Homes / Berkshire Hathaway: 2025 revenue was $12.9 billion, up 4.3%, including homebuilding and financial services; home-sale revenue rose 1.6% while new-home unit sales declined slightly.
Champion Homes: fiscal 2026 net sales were $2.7 billion, up 7.3%; fiscal 2025 US wholesale HUD-code market share was 22.0%.
Cavco Industries: fiscal 2026 net revenue was $2.245 billion, up 11.4%; factory-built housing revenue was $2.157 billion and homes sold rose 5.5% to 20,842.
Legacy Housing: 2025 unit sales were 1,703 homes, focused on lower-price manufactured housing.
current_dynamics: Affordability supports demand because manufactured homes remain far cheaper than site-built housing, but higher mortgage and chattel-loan rates limit buyer qualification. Unit shipments were essentially flat in 2025 and down year to date through May 2026, so revenue resilience is coming more from price, retail mix, finance income and acquisitions than from broad volume growth. Regulatory uncertainty around manufactured-home energy standards eased somewhat after DOE delayed Tier 2 compliance timing in 2025, while zoning reform in states such as Texas could expand addressable land access from September 2026 onward.
whats_growing: Average home prices, multi-section and higher-option homes, captive retail channels, dealer financing, ADUs, community-operator demand, acquisitions by large manufacturers and state-level zoning reforms are growing. Public-company results show larger producers gaining from scale: Champion grew fiscal 2026 net sales 7.3%, and Cavco grew fiscal 2026 factory-built housing revenue 11.6%.
whats_shrinking: Calendar 2025 shipments slipped 0.6% from 2024, and January-May 2026 shipments were 8.0% below the same 2025 period. Modular and panelized site-built completions remain small at a 3% single-family share in 2024, and elevated mortgage rates are shrinking the qualified buyer pool. Smaller independent manufacturers and dealers face pressure from financing constraints, compliance costs and consolidation by Clayton, Champion and Cavco.
recent_developments: 2025-08-28: NAHB reported modular and panelized single-family completions were 28,000 in 2024, just 3% of 1,019,000 total single-family completions.
2026-03-02: Berkshire Hathaway reported Clayton Homes 2025 revenue of $12.9 billion, up 4.3%, while new-home unit sales declined slightly.
2026-05-21: Cavco reported fiscal 2026 net revenue of $2.245 billion, up 11.4%, and record annual homes sold of 20,842.
2026-05-26: Champion Homes reported fiscal 2026 net sales of $2.7 billion, up 7.3%, and adjusted EBITDA of $308.2 million, up 8.1%.
2026-07-02: DOE finalized a delay for Tier 2 manufactured-home energy-standard compliance to 180 days after final enforcement procedures are published.
2026-08-06: Census latest-data page showed manufactured-home shipments data updated through 2026, with 2025 annual shipments at 102,800 and January-May 2026 shipments at 41,400.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is mixed: affordability keeps the value proposition strong, but high rates and tighter lending cap unit growth. Revenue should hold up better than shipments because average prices, multi-section mix, retailer markups, financing income and acquisitions are offsetting weaker volume. Longer term, upside depends on zoning reform, land availability, GSE/chattel-finance access, faster modular adoption by builders and regulatory clarity; downside comes from rate persistence, buyer credit stress, volatile materials and limited consumer acceptance in some jurisdictions.

title: Premium Pet Food Production in the US
one_liner: Premium pet food producers are growing faster than conventional kibble by selling health-led, fresh, refrigerated, freeze-dried and super-premium dog and cat food into omnichannel retail.
overview: Premium pet food producers manufacture higher-margin dog and cat food positioned around superior ingredients, breed or life-stage nutrition, natural claims, fresh or minimally processed formats, and pet health benefits. The baseline industry was estimated at $11.5 billion in 2021 revenue, with dog food representing 70.4% and cat food 29.6% of revenue in 2021. Current demand is still anchored by pet ownership and pet humanization, but 2025-2026 growth is more uneven: total US dog and cat food sales are growing, fresh and refrigerated dog food is outpacing the category, and some shelf-stable dog formats have weakened as consumers respond to higher prices.

key_stats.market_size: Estimated $16.2 billion in 2025 US premium pet food production revenue; broader US pet food sales were estimated at $60.39 billion in 2025, and US pet food and treats spending was projected at $67.8 billion in 2025.
key_stats.growth: Estimated 5.5% 2025 revenue growth for premium pet food production, above total US pet food sales growth of 4.2% in 2025 due to fresh, functional and super-premium mix gains.
key_stats.pet_ownership: 95 million US households owned at least one pet in 2025; dog ownership reached 71 million households and cat ownership reached 53 million households in 2025.
key_stats.fresh_pet_food: Refrigerated/frozen dog food grew 17.8% to $1.6 billion in the 52 weeks ended Aug. 10, 2025; General Mills described fresh pet food as a $3 billion US sub-category in 2025.
key_stats.trade: US dog and cat food exports reached $2.52 billion in 2024, led by Canada, China, Mexico, Japan and Australia.

baseline_2022.market_size: Estimated $11.8 billion in 2022 premium pet food production revenue, derived from the baseline report's 2021 revenue of $11.506 billion and 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 2.33%.
baseline_2022.growth: Estimated 2.33% 2022 growth based on the baseline 2021-2027 projection.
baseline_2022.baseline_context: The baseline file reported 2021 revenue of $11.506 billion, 2021 profit of $2.140 billion, 2021 profit margin of 18.6%, 361 establishments, 333 enterprises, 10,806 employees, $738 million exports and $491 million imports.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling branded and private-label premium dog and cat food to mass merchandisers, supermarkets, pet specialty retailers, club stores, e-commerce platforms, subscription channels and export buyers. Margin comes from brand trust, higher ingredient claims, specialized nutrition, fresh or refrigerated formats, packaging, shelf space, recurring purchases and scale purchasing of meat, poultry, grains, legumes, packaging and logistics.

cost_structure.raw_materials_and_ingredients: Largest cost bucket; includes poultry, meat, seafood, grains, legumes, vitamins, minerals, fats, oils and fresh ingredients. 2024 pet food manufacturers purchased $13.2 billion in farm products across the broader dog and cat food supply chain.
cost_structure.packaging_and_freight: Meaningful cost pressure from cans, pouches, bags, cold-chain handling, warehousing and retailer distribution requirements.
cost_structure.labor: Moderate manufacturing cost; baseline 2021 wages were $663 million across 10,806 employees.
cost_structure.marketing_and_trade_spend: High for premium brands because claims, veterinary credibility, retailer promotion, sampling and digital acquisition support price premiums.
cost_structure.profit: Baseline 2021 profit margin was 18.6%; current margins depend on ingredient inflation, plant utilization, cold-chain costs and mix shift into fresh or functional products.

major_players: Mars Petcare: Royal Canin, Iams, Nutro, Pedigree, Whiskas, Sheba, Cesar, Orijen and Acana through Champion Petfoods.
Nestle Purina PetCare: Purina Pro Plan, ONE, Fancy Feast, Friskies, Merrick and other mass-premium and premium lines.
General Mills: Blue Buffalo and Edgard & Cooper, with Blue Buffalo entering fresh pet food nationally in 2025.
Colgate-Palmolive: Hill's Pet Nutrition, focused on science-led premium and veterinary diets.
Freshpet: refrigerated fresh pet food specialist with 15.2 million US households reached as of 2025.
Post Consumer Brands: Rachael Ray Nutrish, Nature's Recipe, 9Lives, Kibbles 'n Bits, Gravy Train and Perfection Pet Foods co-manufacturing/private-label capacity.
J.M. Smucker: Meow Mix, Milk-Bone, Pup-Peroni and Canine Carry Outs after divesting several pet food brands to Post in 2023.
current_dynamics: The industry is moving from pandemic adoption-driven expansion to a more mature, price-sensitive growth cycle. Pet food remains a protected household staple, but consumers are trading across price tiers, mixing premium food with lower-cost kibble, shopping more through mass and grocery, and using subscriptions for replenishment. Fresh, refrigerated, functional, veterinary, senior, digestive, weight-management and cat-focused formulas are gaining share, while conventional dry and wet dog food faced sales declines in measured channels during 2025.
whats_growing: Fresh, refrigerated and frozen dog food, with 17.8% growth to $1.6 billion in the 52 weeks ended Aug. 10, 2025.

Functional nutrition, supplements and condition-specific formulas; 2025 dog supplement sales grew 9.2% to $633 million and cat supplement sales grew 27.9% to $53.1 million in Circana-measured channels.
Cat food, supported by 53 million US cat-owning households in 2025 and 5% year-over-year cat ownership growth.
E-commerce, omnichannel and subscription purchasing; 52% of pet parents reported using subscription-based purchasing in 2024, including 31% for pet food.
Private label and value-premium options as inflation-fatigued consumers seek lower prices without abandoning nutrition claims.
whats_shrinking: Measured dry dog food sales declined 2.9% to $14.2 billion in the 52 weeks ended Aug. 10, 2025.
Measured wet dog food sales declined 3.6% to $3.9 billion in the 52 weeks ended Aug. 10, 2025.
Measured semi-moist dog food sales declined 9.2% to $118 million in the 52 weeks ended Aug. 10, 2025.
Measured semi-moist cat food sales declined 10.0% to $14 million in the 52 weeks ended Aug. 10, 2025.
Undifferentiated premium claims are losing pricing power as shoppers compare value, ingredient credibility and functional benefits.
recent_developments: 2024-10-01: The FDA-AAFCO ingredient-definition MOU expired, pushing animal food ingredient review toward a new FDA transition framework.
2025-04-07: PFI and IFEEDER reported $51.7 billion in 2024 US dog and cat food sales and 9.8 million tons of production using 600+ ingredients.
2025-06-23: General Mills announced Blue Buffalo Love Made Fresh and a US launch of Edgard & Cooper through PetSmart.
2025-10-21: Blue Buffalo launched Love Made Fresh nationally, entering the $3 billion US fresh pet food sub-category.
2025-10-28: Pet Food Processing reported 2025 Circana data showing refrigerated/frozen dog food up 17.8% while several shelf-stable dog categories declined.
2026-03-26: APPA reported $158 billion in 2025 total US pet industry expenditures and projected $165 billion in 2026.
outlook: Premium pet food production should keep expanding through 2026-2029, but the mix matters more than headline pet ownership. Growth is likely to outpace conventional pet food where producers can prove health, convenience, freshness, veterinary credibility or value, while brands dependent on standard dry and wet dog food face share pressure. Manufacturing winners will be companies with trusted brands, cold-chain or co-manufacturing capacity, ingredient procurement scale, omnichannel distribution and enough price architecture to serve both affluent pet parents and value-seeking households.

title: Premium Steak Restaurants
one_liner: Premium steak restaurants are high-check, full-service dining concepts built around prime beef, wine, business dining and special-occasion meals.
overview: Premium steak restaurants include chain, franchised and independent full-service restaurants where guests order while seated and pay after eating, with menus centered on higher-quality steak cuts, alcoholic beverages, sides, seafood and celebration-oriented service. The baseline IBIS file defined the segment as high-end steak establishments with average checks of $50 or more and estimated 2021 revenue at $5.2 billion. Current public 2025 reporting citing IBISWorld places industry revenue at $8.3 billion after a 2020-2025 CAGR of 5.4%, indicating the post-pandemic rebound was stronger than the older 2021 outlook. Demand is concentrated among households earning over $100,000, corporate dining, travel-heavy urban markets and special-occasion guests, while profitability depends on managing beef procurement, skilled labor, rent and beverage mix.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $8.3 billion in US premium steak restaurant revenue, cited from IBISWorld in 2025 reporting.
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025: 5.4% CAGR in industry revenue, cited from IBISWorld in 2025 reporting.
key_stats.establishments: 2025: 4,263 US premium steakhouse establishments, cited from IBISWorld in 2025 reporting.
key_stats.full_service_context: 2025: US full-service foodservice sales were $488.4 billion in 2025 dollars, according to USDA ERS.
key_stats.food_away_from_home_share: 2025: food away from home represented 56.3% of total US food expenditures, according to USDA ERS.
key_stats.input_pressure: 2026: USDA ERS raised the 2026 slaughter steer price forecast to $251.10 per cwt and 2027 to $254.25 per cwt.
key_stats.menu_inflation: May 2025-May 2026: BLS reported full-service meals and snacks prices up 3.8%.
key_stats.profitability_signal: 2026: Darden's Fine Dining segment posted 17.7% segment profit margin in fiscal 2026, down 90 basis points from fiscal 2025.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimate: $5.4 billion, inferred from the baseline file's 2021 revenue of $5.191 billion and its 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 4.3%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimate: +4.3%, using the baseline file's projected 2021-2026 annualized revenue growth rate.
baseline_2022.baseline_source: Baseline file last updated Nov. 30, 2021; figures were in 2021 dollars and projected 2026 revenue of $6.4 billion.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2021: 3.7% EBIT margin in the baseline file; baseline projected 2026 margin of 4.1%.
baseline_2022.employment: 2021: 93,993 employees in the baseline file; baseline projected 116,168 employees by 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn revenue from dine-in steak entrees, appetizers, sides, desserts, wine, cocktails, private dining, corporate events, gift cards and a smaller amount of takeout or delivery. High margins generally come from beverage programs, premium add-ons, seafood towers, prix fixe menus and special-occasion spending, while steak itself is a traffic and brand anchor with volatile input costs.
cost_structure: The largest expenses are food and beverage purchases, labor, occupancy and restaurant operating costs. Texas Roadhouse reported 2025 food and beverage costs equal to 35.0% of restaurant and other sales and labor equal to 33.3%, showing how beef and staffing dominate steakhouse economics. Darden reported in fiscal 2026 that higher food and beverage costs reduced LongHorn margins and that higher labor plus food and beverage costs reduced Fine Dining margins. Smaller independent premium steakhouses face weaker purchasing leverage than national chains and are more exposed to spot beef prices, rent in prime urban locations and wage inflation.
major_players: Darden Restaurants: LongHorn Steakhouse, The Capital Grille and Ruth's Chris Steak House
Texas Roadhouse
Bloomin' Brands: Outback Steakhouse and Fleming's Prime Steakhouse & Wine Bar
Landry's: Mastro's, Morton's and Saltgrass Steak House
Fogo de Chao
STK Steakhouse and ONE Group Hospitality
Independent and regional upscale steakhouses
current_dynamics: The industry is benefiting from affluent consumers still paying for experience-led dining, business meals and celebration occasions, while value-oriented steak concepts are taking share from weaker full-service peers. The 2026 constraint is not demand alone but margin: cattle supply remains tight, beef prices are elevated, full-service menu prices are still rising and labor costs remain sticky. Chains with purchasing scale, reservation data, loyalty programs and menu engineering are better positioned than independents. Premium concepts are also broadening beyond steak with seafood, wine dinners, mocktails, bar traffic and prix fixe offers to protect traffic without discounting their core brand.
whats_growing: Growing areas include affluent special-occasion dining, corporate/private dining, premium beef upgrades such as Prime, dry-aged and Wagyu cuts, wine and cocktail programs, Brazilian-style steakhouses, suburban high-income expansion, gift cards, loyalty-driven reservations and menu bundles that let guests trade up from an advertised entry price.
whats_shrinking: Shrinking or pressured areas include lower-margin steak cuts exposed to commodity inflation, weaker urban independents with high rent, traffic from price-sensitive middle-income diners, late-night dining in some downtown markets, concepts unable to staff consistently and restaurants without purchasing scale or beverage mix to offset beef costs.
recent_developments: 2025-07-28: Public reporting citing IBISWorld estimated US premium steak restaurant revenue at $8.3 billion in 2025 and 4,263 establishments.
2026-02-25: Bloomin' Brands reported fiscal 2025 Outback comparable sales down 0.5% and Fleming's up 2.5%, while guiding 2026 US comparable sales to +0.5% to +2.5%.
2026-02-25: Bloomin' Brands said its 2026 outlook assumed commodity inflation of 4.5% to 5.5% and labor inflation of 3.0% to 3.5%.
2026-06-25: Darden reported fiscal 2026 LongHorn sales of $3.423 billion, up 13.1%, and Fine Dining sales of $1.376 billion, up 5.4%.
2026-07-17: USDA ERS raised the 2026 slaughter steer price forecast to $251.10 per cwt and the 2027 forecast to $254.25 per cwt.
2026-08-05: Bloomin' Brands reported stronger Q2 2026 results as Outback diners traded up to pricier steak combinations, lifting Outback same-store sales by 1.4%.
outlook: The 2026-2027 outlook is cautiously positive for revenue and mixed for margins. Nominal sales should keep growing because menu prices remain higher, full-service dining demand is stable among affluent households and major chains continue opening units. Real traffic growth is likely more uneven, with premium concepts relying on corporate events, holidays, private rooms and beverage attach rates. Beef availability and cattle prices are the main downside risk; operators with scale, disciplined menus and strong guest experience can hold margin better than single-location competitors.

title: Prepaid Credit & Debit Card Providers
one_liner: Prepaid card providers issue open-loop cards and accounts that let consumers, employers and businesses spend stored value without traditional credit underwriting.
overview: Industry revenue is estimated at $17.6 billion in 2025, derived from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $15.771 billion and its 2022-2027 forecast CAGR of 3.7%. Demand remains tied to underbanked consumers, younger users, payroll cards, tax-refund and government disbursements, retail reload networks and online shopping. The Federal Reserve's 2026 release shows prepaid debit card payments at 21.3 billion transactions and $0.65 trillion in value in 2024, including 11.8 billion general-purpose prepaid transactions worth $0.43 trillion. Growth is shifting away from traditional rack-sold general-purpose reloadable cards toward embedded finance, wage access, tax processing, corporate rewards, instant disbursements and digital wallets.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated industry revenue: $17.6 billion, in 2022 dollars
key_stats.transaction_volume: 2024 prepaid debit card payments: 21.3 billion transactions
key_stats.transaction_value: 2024 prepaid debit card payment value: $0.65 trillion
key_stats.general_purpose_prepaid: 2024 general-purpose prepaid debit: 11.8 billion transactions and $0.43 trillion in value
key_stats.consumer_base: 2023 US households using prepaid cards: 5.9%; 2023 unbanked households: 4.2%, or 5.6 million households
key_stats.ecommerce_driver: 2025 US retail e-commerce sales, seasonally adjusted: $1.231 trillion; Q1 2026: $326.740 billion

baseline_2022.revenue_mix: 2022 revenue: 60.3% card fees, 25.6% interchange fees, 14.1% cash transfer and reload services

how_it_makes_money: Providers earn revenue from activation, monthly maintenance, ATM, replacement, paper statement, bill pay, foreign transaction and other cardholder fees; merchant-paid interchange on purchases; cash reload and money-transfer fees; program-management fees from partners; payroll, tax-refund, government-benefit, incentives and corporate-disbursement programs; and interest income on customer balances where permitted. In 2022, the baseline mix was 60.3% card fees, 25.6% interchange and 14.1% reload or transfer services.
cost_structure: The largest costs are payment processing, network access, issuing-bank sponsorship, fraud losses, customer service, compliance, KYC/AML monitoring, technology, retail distribution commissions, marketing and wages. Green Dot's 2025 company-wide cost profile illustrates the pressure: processing expenses were $1.230 billion, compensation and benefits were $254.4 million, sales and marketing were $207.9 million, and G&A was $352.0 million against $2.080 billion of operating revenue.

Netspend / Ouro
Blackhawk Network
Pathward, N.A.
InComm Payments
The Bancorp Bank
Republic Bank & Trust Company
Fiserv and other processing or embedded-finance platform providers
current_dynamics: The market is expanding in transaction count but not uniformly in provider economics. The Fed's 2024 data show general-purpose prepaid transactions growing at a 2021-2024 CAGR of 9.7% by number and 4.3% by value, while all prepaid debit grew only 4.0% by number and 1.5% by value because EBT volumes contracted after pandemic-era benefits rolled off. Consumer-facing retail GPR cards face migration to mobile bank accounts and payment apps; Green Dot reported 2025 pressure in traditional retail distribution and direct-to-consumer channels, while embedded finance, tax processing, money movement and BaaS were stronger. Compliance and fraud remain central operating constraints after the Federal Reserve's 2024 $44 million Green Dot enforcement action and 2025 CFPB actions against payments companies for error-resolution and fraud-handling failures.
whats_growing: General-purpose prepaid usage: 2024 transactions reached 11.8 billion, up from 9.0 billion in 2021
Digital and embedded finance programs tied to payroll, tax refunds, earned wage access, gig-worker payouts and partner-branded accounts
Corporate rewards and incentives, with Blackhawk Network citing 2026 platform scale of $30 billion in annual load value and about 1 billion cards issued annually
Contactless and wallet-enabled prepaid products, including 2025 tap-to-pay Visa gift card launches
Retail e-commerce, with 2025 seasonally adjusted sales totaling about $1.231 trillion
whats_shrinking: Electronic benefits transfer card activity after pandemic-era support: 2021-2024 EBT prepaid transactions declined at a -16.9% CAGR
Traditional rack-sold consumer reloadable-card economics as users migrate to digital bank accounts and P2P apps
Some legacy prepaid brands, including Serve American Express Prepaid Debit Accounts, which stopped spending on June 2, 2026 and closed on June 3, 2026
Prepaid card household penetration: FDIC reported 5.9% of US households using prepaid cards in 2023, down from 6.9% in 2021
Fee-heavy card plans as competitors use lower monthly fees, direct-deposit waivers and bundled digital-banking features
recent_developments: 2025-01-16: CFPB ordered Block/Cash App to pay up to $120 million in consumer redress and a $55 million penalty for fraud and EFTA error-resolution failures.
2025-06-09: Blackhawk Network announced a Tap to Pay Visa Gift Card for summer 2025 with tamper-evident packaging and wallet integration.
2025-11-24: Green Dot announced strategic transactions with Smith Ventures and CommerceOne, including a $690 million sale of non-bank fintech operations and separation of Green Dot Bank.
2026-03-16: Green Dot reported 2025 operating revenue of $2.080 billion, up 21% from 2024, with 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $173.6 million.
2026-06-03: Serve American Express Prepaid Debit Accounts were officially closed after the June 2, 2026 final spend date.
2026-07-01: Federal Reserve Payments Study released 2024 top-line data showing 21.3 billion prepaid debit transactions worth $0.65 trillion.
outlook: Revenue is expected to keep growing at a low- to mid-single-digit pace through 2027, reaching roughly $18.9 billion under the 2022 baseline projection. Upside comes from embedded finance, instant disbursements, payroll cards, tax-refund products, corporate rewards, digital wallet integration and higher e-commerce transaction volume. Downside risks include lower household use of prepaid cards, competition from free checking and payment apps, interchange and fee pressure, fraud losses, AML costs, sponsor-bank scrutiny and consumer-protection enforcement. The best-positioned providers will combine low-cost digital accounts, broad cash-reload networks, strong compliance infrastructure and partner distribution.

title: Prepared Frozen Fish Production
one_liner: U.S. prepared frozen fish producers turn fish, shellfish and surimi into frozen fillets, sticks, meals, shrimp products, soups and other value-added seafood for grocery, club, foodservice and institutional buyers.
overview: The industry processes fish and seafood into prepared frozen products, including battered or breaded fish fillets and sticks, shrimp items, seafood burgers, surimi and prepared frozen meals. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline put U.S. industry revenue at $9.5 billion and projected modest expansion to $10.2 billion by 2026, while current 2025 retail data show frozen seafood remains a large but price-sensitive category: Circana-based reporting placed latest-52-week frozen seafood dollar sales at $8.4 billion in 2025, up 2.8%, with units up only 0.5%. NOAA reported 2023 U.S. seafood consumption at 19.1 pounds per capita and estimated that 80% of seafood eaten in the United States came from imports, underscoring both demand breadth and import exposure.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: about $10.2 billion in U.S. prepared frozen fish production revenue, based on the IBISWorld 2021-2026 industry forecast; 2025 retail frozen seafood sales were $8.4 billion in the latest 52 weeks reported by Circana/Progressive Grocer.
key_stats.growth: 2025: retail frozen seafood dollar sales +2.8% year over year and unit sales +0.5%; 2026: industry revenue is best characterized as low-single-digit growth, consistent with the older IBISWorld 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 1.3%.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2026: IBISWorld baseline forecast profit margin of 2.7%, down from 2.8% in 2021.
key_stats.imports: 2023: NOAA estimated 80% of seafood consumed in the United States came from foreign imports; 2026 IBISWorld baseline forecast prepared frozen fish imports at about $2.2 billion.
key_stats.producer_prices: 2026: BLS/FRED seafood product preparation and packaging PPI reached 154.691 in June 2026, up from 147.426 in January 2026.
key_stats.consumption: 2023: U.S. per capita seafood consumption was 19.1 pounds, according to NOAA Fisheries.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $9.6 billion, estimated from the 2021 IBISWorld baseline revenue of $9.525 billion and its 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 1.3%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 1.3% implied baseline growth, using the IBISWorld 2021-2026 forecast path.
baseline_2022.imports: 2022: roughly $2.1 billion to $2.2 billion implied from the IBISWorld baseline import path of $2.088 billion in 2021 to $2.2 billion in 2026.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022: about 2.8%, near the 2021 baseline of 2.8% and above the 2026 forecast of 2.7%.

how_it_makes_money: Producers buy wild-caught and farmed seafood, process it through freezing, breading, battering, seasoning, portioning, forming, packaging and cold-chain distribution, then sell branded and private-label products to supermarkets, club stores, broadline distributors, restaurants, school lunch and government food programs. Revenue is driven by seafood input prices, value-added processing, product innovation, freezer-shelf placement, foodservice contracts and the ability to pass freight, labor, packaging and compliance costs into wholesale prices.
cost_structure: Major costs are seafood raw materials, especially pollock, cod, salmon, shrimp and crab; cold storage and refrigerated transportation; plant labor; breading, oils, sauces and packaging; energy for freezing; quality assurance and food-safety systems; trade compliance and traceability; marketing and slotting fees for retail brands. The baseline industry had thin margins, with profit near 2.8% of revenue in 2021 and 2.7% forecast for 2026, so swings in seafood costs, tariffs, freight and labor can quickly compress earnings.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions: retail and foodservice still value frozen seafood for convenience, protein content, long shelf life and lower waste, but inflation has made consumers more selective. Frozen seafood dollars rose in 2025 even as units were nearly flat, indicating price-led growth rather than broad volume expansion. Import reliance remains high, and tariffs, antidumping duties, Russian-origin restrictions and NOAA/FDA traceability initiatives are raising procurement and compliance complexity. Domestic manufacturers with brands, private-label scale, cold-chain relationships and automated plants are better positioned than small processors.
whats_growing: Frozen finfish, pollock-based fried products, salmon items, air-fryer-ready seafood, premium and ultra-premium frozen seafood, private label, globally seasoned products, value-added shrimp, foodservice and school/institutional fish sticks, and products positioned around protein, omega-3s, wild-caught sourcing and convenience are growing. Gorton's 2025 Indiana plant opening signals confidence in U.S. demand for prepared frozen seafood capacity.
whats_shrinking: Price-sensitive shellfish volumes, commodity frozen shrimp when tariff and duty costs rise, low-differentiation breaded items, products dependent on high-risk or sanctioned supply chains, and smaller operators without traceability systems or cold-chain scale are under pressure. Circana-based 2025 reporting showed frozen seafood unit sales only up 0.5% despite dollar growth, and late-2025 seafood inflation weighed on volume.
recent_developments: 2025-03: FMI reported U.S. seafood retail sales had stepped back since 2022, with 2024 seafood dollar sales down 1.2% while units rose 1.0%.
2025-08: FDA proposed extending the FSMA Food Traceability Rule compliance date by 30 months, affecting seafood supply-chain recordkeeping plans.
2025-10: Nissui announced Gorton's opened a new Lebanon, Indiana production plant that began operations in mid-September 2025 to expand prepared frozen seafood capacity.
2025-12: Progressive Grocer reported Circana latest-52-week frozen seafood dollar sales of $8.4 billion, up 2.8%, with unit sales up 0.5%.
2026-03: NOAA released 2023 Fisheries of the United States highlights showing 19.1 pounds of per capita seafood consumption and 80% import reliance.
2026-06: USITC voted to keep the antidumping order on certain frozen fish fillets from Vietnam after its sunset review.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is for modest nominal growth, with real volume growth limited by high seafood prices and cautious consumers. Frozen seafood should remain resilient because it solves convenience, waste and availability problems better than fresh seafood, but producers will need to defend margins through automation, sourcing diversification, private-label scale, product premiumization and disciplined pricing. Regulatory and trade complexity is likely to favor larger processors with digital traceability and import-compliance capacity. If seafood inflation eases, volume could improve; if tariffs, duties or supply shocks intensify, revenue may rise from pricing while pounds sold remain flat or down.
